title: Night Sweats After Drinking: Causes, Fixes, and When to Worry
excerpt: Why you wake up hot and soaked after drinking, how to tell normal hangover sweats from withdrawal warning signs, what helps, and when to see a doctor.
metaDescription: Why you wake up sweating after drinking, how to tell hangover sweats from withdrawal signs, how to stop them, and when night sweats need a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** waking up hot, damp, or soaked after a night of drinking is common, and for most social drinkers it's a normal, short-lived effect of alcohol. Alcohol opens up the blood vessels in your skin, nudges your heart rate up, and wrecks the second half of your sleep. As your body clears the alcohol overnight, your nervous system rebounds into a more alert state, and sweating is one of the ways that shows up. A sweaty night after a big evening usually settles within a day.

There is one pattern you shouldn't brush off. If you drink heavily most days and start sweating (along with shaking, anxiety, or a racing heart) when you cut back or stop, that can be **alcohol withdrawal**, which is a medical issue, not a hangover. This guide explains the difference, the main causes of sweating after drinking, what helps, and when to see a doctor.

> **When to see a doctor.** This article is general information, not medical advice. **Get emergency care (call 911 in the US) if** sweating comes with confusion, hallucinations (seeing, hearing, or feeling things that aren't there), a seizure, chest pain, fainting, a very fast or irregular heartbeat, trouble breathing, or vomiting you can't stop. **Talk to a doctor soon if** you get sweats, shaky hands, anxiety, or nausea when you cut back after drinking heavily most days, if night sweats happen on nights you haven't been drinking, if they come with fever, unexplained weight loss, or swollen glands, or if you sweat and flush after only a small amount of alcohol. If you drink heavily every day, **don't stop suddenly on your own** without talking to a doctor first, because withdrawal can be dangerous and is much safer with medical help.

## Why Do I Sweat When I Drink? The Main Causes

Sweating after alcohol rarely has a single cause. Usually several of these stack up on the same night.

### 1. Alcohol warms your skin and dumps heat

Alcohol is a vasodilator, which means it relaxes and widens blood vessels, especially the small ones near the surface of your skin. More warm blood flows to your skin, which is why your face and chest can feel flushed and hot after a few drinks. Your body reads that warmth as overheating and responds the way it always does: by sweating to cool down.

This is also why the "warming" feeling of a drink is misleading. You feel warmer, but you're actually losing heat faster. In a warm bedroom under a heavy duvet, that same mechanism turns into a damp pillow.

### 2. Your heart rate and metabolism speed up

Alcohol tends to push your heart rate up, both while you're drinking and for hours afterward. Your liver is also busy breaking alcohol down, first into a compound called acetaldehyde and then into acetate. A faster heart and a busy metabolism both produce heat. Some people notice a pounding or racing heart in bed after drinking, and sweating often comes along with it.

### 3. The overnight rebound (a mini version of withdrawal)

This is the cause most people don't know about, and it explains why sweats so often hit in the early hours rather than right after you fall asleep.

Alcohol acts as a depressant on the brain. It boosts the calming signals from a brain messenger called GABA and dampens the excitatory signals from another called glutamate. Your brain pushes back against that by turning its own "alert" systems up a little. When the alcohol wears off overnight, the depressant effect is gone but the pushback is still there for a while. The result is a short burst of nervous-system activation: lighter, broken sleep, a faster heartbeat, anxiety, and sweating.

Researchers sometimes describe a hangover as a mild, short version of withdrawal for exactly this reason. It's normal, it's temporary, and in a social drinker it fades as the brain rebalances over the next day. It's the same rebound that drives "hangxiety," the anxious, on-edge feeling many people get the morning after (our [hangxiety guide](/never-hungover/hangxiety-complete-guide-2026-supplements-research) covers that side of it).

### 4. Broken sleep and REM rebound

Alcohol helps many people fall asleep faster, but it makes the second half of the night worse. Early on it suppresses REM sleep, the dream-heavy stage. Later in the night, as the alcohol clears, REM tends to come back in a burst, along with more waking, vivid dreams, and restless sleep. Sweating, waking up hot, and kicking off the covers all fit this pattern. Our [deep dive on alcohol and REM sleep](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-rem-sleep-complete-scientific-analysis-2025) explains the sleep science in more detail.

### 5. Low blood sugar

While your liver is processing alcohol, it's less able to release stored sugar into your bloodstream. If you drank on an empty stomach or skipped dinner, your blood sugar can dip overnight or by morning. Low blood sugar triggers adrenaline, and adrenaline causes sweating, shakiness, and a racing heart. This is one reason a proper meal before drinking makes such a difference. People with diabetes, especially those on insulin or certain tablets, are at higher risk of serious lows after drinking and should follow their own doctor's advice.

### 6. Dehydration (yes, even though you're sweating)

Alcohol makes you pee more by suppressing a hormone that normally tells your kidneys to hold onto water. Add sweating on top and you can wake up dehydrated. Dehydration makes it harder for your body to regulate temperature smoothly and can add to the headache, thirst, and clammy feeling the next morning.

### 7. The bedroom itself

It sounds obvious, but it matters. A warm room, a heavy duvet, synthetic sheets, or sharing a bed all make alcohol-related sweating worse. Alcohol makes you less sensitive to how warm you are until you're already overheated, so you may not wake up to kick the blanket off until you're soaked.

## Night Sweats After One Night of Drinking

If you mostly drink socially and you're searching this because you woke up drenched after one big night, the most likely explanation is a combination of the warming effect on your skin, the overnight rebound, and broken sleep. A few things make it more likely:

- **Drinking more than usual**, or drinking quickly.
- **Drinking close to bedtime**, so a lot of alcohol is still in your system when you fall asleep.
- **Drinking on an empty stomach.**
- **A warm room or heavy bedding.**
- **Mixing alcohol with other things** that affect sleep or temperature, such as sleeping pills, antihistamines, or stimulants like energy drinks.

This kind of sweating usually happens that night and the next morning, then settles as the alcohol clears and you rest, eat, and rehydrate. It isn't a sign of damage, and it doesn't mean you have a problem with alcohol. It's your body telling you the night was a bit much.

## Night Sweats Days After Drinking: When It's Something Else

This is the section to read carefully, because the timing and the pattern tell you a lot.

**Normal hangover sweating** happens the night of drinking and the next morning, and improves within a day.

**Withdrawal-related sweating** is different. It tends to show up in people who have been drinking heavily on most days for weeks or longer, and it begins when they cut back or stop. Symptoms usually start somewhere between several hours and a day after the last drink, and can build over the following days. Along with sweating, common signs include:

- Shaky or trembling hands
- Anxiety, restlessness, or irritability
- A fast heartbeat
- Nausea or vomiting
- Trouble sleeping, often with vivid dreams
- Feeling much better after a drink

That last point is an important clue. If a drink in the morning "fixes" the sweats and the shakes, the body has likely adapted to alcohol being there all the time.

In more severe cases, withdrawal can lead to hallucinations, seizures, or a dangerous state called delirium tremens, which involves severe confusion, high fever, and a racing heart. This is why medical guidance is clear that people who drink heavily every day **should not quit suddenly on their own**. A doctor can assess the risk and, where needed, use medication to make stopping safe. If you or someone with you has confusion, hallucinations, or a seizure after stopping drinking, that's an emergency: call 911 (in the US) or go to the nearest emergency department.

None of this is meant to alarm someone who had one heavy weekend. It's here because the same symptom, sweating, can mean very different things depending on how much and how often you've been drinking. If you aren't sure which side of the line you're on, a short, honest conversation with a doctor is the quickest way to find out. Doctors hear this every day and are there to help, not judge.

## Cold Sweats With a Hangover

Some people don't wake up hot. They wake up clammy, pale, and cold, with sweat on their skin even though they feel chilly. That's usually your stress response at work rather than heat.

The usual triggers are:

- **Low blood sugar**, which releases adrenaline.
- **Nausea**, which on its own often brings on a cold sweat (think of how you feel just before being sick).
- **Dehydration**, which can make you lightheaded, especially when you stand up.
- **The nervous-system rebound** described above.

Simple steps tend to help: sip water or an electrolyte drink, eat something gentle with carbohydrates (toast, crackers, a banana), and rest lying down if you feel faint. If cold sweats come with chest pain, fainting, confusion, a very fast or irregular heartbeat, or vomiting that won't stop, don't wait it out. Get medical help.

## Sweating and Flushing After Very Little Alcohol

If you turn red, feel hot, get a pounding heart, or start sweating after only one drink, the cause may be different from a normal hangover.

- **Alcohol flush reaction.** Many people, especially of East Asian descent, carry a variant of the ALDH2 gene that slows the breakdown of acetaldehyde, the toxic first breakdown product of alcohol. Acetaldehyde builds up and causes flushing, warmth, a fast heartbeat, and sometimes nausea or sweating. It's worth knowing about because acetaldehyde is linked to cancer risk in people with this variant who drink regularly. Our [complete guide to Asian flush](/never-hungover/complete-guide-asian-flush-comprehensive) goes through it in detail.
- **Reactions to other ingredients.** Some people react to histamine in red wine, sulfites, or other components of specific drinks. If one particular drink sets you off while others don't, that's a clue.
- **Medication interactions.** A few medicines cause a strong reaction with alcohol, including disulfiram (a drug used specifically to make alcohol unpleasant), and some people react when drinking while on certain antibiotics such as metronidazole. Many antidepressants can cause night sweats on their own, and alcohol can make sleep and sweating worse. Check the label or ask a pharmacist about any medicine you take regularly.

If you get a sudden, strong reaction to small amounts of alcohol, especially with hives, swelling of the lips or throat, wheezing, or trouble breathing, treat it as an emergency.

## Other Things That Can Make Sweats Worse After Drinking

A few other common situations deserve a mention:

- **Snoring and sleep apnea.** Alcohol relaxes the muscles of your throat, which makes snoring and pauses in breathing more likely. Sleep apnea is linked to night sweats and broken sleep. If a partner says you snore loudly or seem to stop breathing, especially after drinking, it's worth raising with a doctor.
- **Perimenopause and menopause.** Many people notice that alcohol, especially in the evening, makes hot flashes and night sweats worse. Cutting back or stopping earlier in the evening is a common first step, and a doctor can talk through other options.
- **Infections and illness.** If you're coming down with something, alcohol can add to fever and sweating. Night sweats with a fever that doesn't go away need a doctor.
- **Other stimulants.** Energy drinks mixed with alcohol, nicotine, and some recreational drugs raise heart rate and body temperature and can make sweating much worse.

### Night sweats that aren't about alcohol at all

If you get regular night sweats on nights you haven't been drinking, alcohol probably isn't the whole story. Night sweats have many causes, including hormonal changes, an overactive thyroid, some medications, anxiety, and infections, and less commonly more serious conditions. Night sweats together with unexplained weight loss, ongoing fever, swollen glands, or a persistent cough should be checked by a doctor.

## How to Stop Night Sweats After Drinking

There's no trick that cancels out the effects of alcohol on your body. What works is reducing the amount of alcohol left in your system at bedtime and making it easier for your body to stay cool.

### Before and while you drink

- **Eat a real meal first.** Food slows how fast alcohol reaches your bloodstream and helps keep your blood sugar steadier overnight.
- **Pace yourself.** Your body clears roughly one standard drink per hour, though it varies a lot between people. Spacing drinks out keeps your peak level lower.
- **Alternate with water.** A glass of water between drinks slows you down and helps with hydration.
- **Stop a few hours before bed.** This is one of the most useful changes. The more alcohol you've cleared before you fall asleep, the smaller the overnight rebound.
- **Skip the energy-drink mixers.** Caffeine and stimulants on top of alcohol make a hot, wired, sweaty night more likely.

Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) walks through these habits and the evidence behind them.

### Before bed

- **Drink some water,** but you don't need to force down a huge amount. A glass or two is plenty for most people.
- **Have a light snack** if you didn't eat much, especially something with carbohydrates, to help keep blood sugar from dipping.
- **Cool the room.** A cooler bedroom, an open window, or a fan makes a real difference.
- **Use lighter bedding** and breathable cotton or linen sheets. Keep a lighter blanket nearby in case you get cold later.
- **Don't add sleeping pills or sedating antihistamines** to alcohol. Combining sedatives makes you more impaired and can affect your breathing.

### If you wake up drenched

- **Change into dry clothes** and swap the pillowcase if you need to, so you don't get chilled.
- **Sip water or an electrolyte drink.** If you're curious about timing, we cover it in our guide to [electrolytes before or after drinking](/never-hungover/electrolytes-before-or-after-drinking).
- **Eat something simple** in the morning.
- **Rest.** Your nervous system rebalances over the day. Light movement and fresh air often help more than you'd expect.
- **Avoid "hair of the dog."** Another drink may quiet the rebound for a little while, but it only pushes the symptoms later. If you feel you *need* a drink to stop sweating or shaking, that's a reason to talk to a doctor.

## A Quick Way to Tell What's Going On

| What you notice | Most likely explanation | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| Hot and sweaty in the early hours after a big night, fine by the next day | Normal hangover effects: warm skin, overnight rebound, broken sleep | Cool room, water, food, rest; drink less and stop earlier next time |
| Cold, clammy sweat in the morning with nausea or shakiness | Low blood sugar, dehydration, stress response | Fluids, gentle carbohydrates, rest |
| Flushing, heat, and sweating after one drink | Flush reaction, ingredient sensitivity, or a medication interaction | Check medicines; talk to a doctor if it's new or strong |
| Sweats plus shaky hands and anxiety when you cut back after drinking heavily most days | Possible alcohol withdrawal | Talk to a doctor before stopping; don't quit suddenly on your own |
| Confusion, hallucinations, seizure, or chest pain | Emergency | Call 911 (US) or go to the emergency department |
| Night sweats on nights you didn't drink, or with fever or weight loss | Probably not alcohol-related | See a doctor |

## What About Supplements?

You'll find plenty of products sold as hangover fixes. It's worth being straight about what they can and can't do for sweating.

- **Electrolyte drinks** can help you rehydrate, which may make you feel better the morning after. They don't stop the overnight rebound.
- **Magnesium** is popular for sleep and relaxation. Evidence for it as a hangover remedy is limited.
- **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a compound from the Japanese raisin tree (Hovenia dulcis) that has drawn interest for its effects on how alcohol acts in the brain. A widely cited 2012 study in *The Journal of Neuroscience* found that DHM reduced alcohol intoxication and some withdrawal-like signs in rats, apparently through the GABA system involved in the rebound described above. That's interesting, but it's animal research, and human data are limited. **There is no good evidence that DHM prevents or treats night sweats**, and it is not a treatment for alcohol withdrawal.

If you'd like to try DHM as part of a sensible drinking routine (eating first, pacing yourself, stopping well before bed), well-reviewed options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the lower-cost [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people typically take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. If you take regular medication, check with a pharmacist first.

No supplement replaces the basics, and none should be used to keep drinking through warning signs. If your sweats are part of a pattern of heavy daily drinking, a doctor is the right next step.

## The Bottom Line

- Night sweats after drinking are common and, after an occasional big night, usually harmless. They come from alcohol warming your skin, raising your heart rate, disrupting sleep, and the nervous-system rebound as it wears off.
- Drinking less, eating first, stopping a few hours before bed, and keeping the bedroom cool are the most effective fixes.
- Cold, clammy sweats the next morning usually point to low blood sugar, nausea, or dehydration. Fluids, food, and rest help.
- Sweating with shaking, anxiety, or a racing heart when you cut back after drinking heavily most days can be withdrawal. Talk to a doctor, and don't stop suddenly on your own.
- Confusion, hallucinations, seizures, chest pain, or fainting are emergencies. Night sweats on nights you didn't drink, or with fever or weight loss, need a doctor's check.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Why do I get night sweats after drinking alcohol?**

Alcohol widens the blood vessels in your skin, which makes you feel warm and pushes heat out through your skin. It also speeds up your heart rate, and as your body clears the alcohol in the second half of the night, your nervous system swings into a more alert, 'revved up' state that can trigger sweating. Poor sleep, a warm room, heavy bedding, and low blood sugar can add to it. For most social drinkers, an occasional sweaty night after a big evening is one of these normal effects.

**Is it normal to sweat at night after just one night of drinking?**

Yes, it's common. After a heavier-than-usual night, many people wake up hot, clammy, or soaked around 3 to 5 a.m. That's usually the rebound that happens as the sedating effect of alcohol wears off, combined with alcohol's warming effect on the skin. If it only happens after bigger nights and goes away within a day, it is usually not a sign of anything serious.

**Are night sweats after drinking a sign of alcohol withdrawal?**

They can be, depending on the pattern. One sweaty night after a single big evening is usually just a hangover effect. Sweating that shows up when you stop or cut back after drinking heavily most days for weeks or longer, especially with shaking hands, anxiety, a racing heart, or nausea that eases when you drink again, can be a withdrawal sign. If that sounds like you, talk to a doctor before stopping, because withdrawal can become dangerous and doctors can make it safer.

**How long do night sweats last after drinking?**

For a typical night out, sweating usually happens during the night and the following morning, and settles once the alcohol has cleared and you've rested and rehydrated, usually within a day. Sweats that last several days after you stop drinking, get worse instead of better, or come with tremors, confusion, or hallucinations are not a normal hangover and need medical attention.

**How can I stop night sweats after drinking?**

The most reliable fix is drinking less and stopping a few hours before bed so more of the alcohol clears before you sleep. Alternate alcoholic drinks with water, eat a proper meal, keep the bedroom cool, use lighter bedding, and avoid stacking alcohol with sleeping pills or antihistamines. If you flush red or sweat after only a small amount, or the sweats are getting more frequent, check in with a doctor.

**Why do I get cold sweats with a hangover?**

Cold, clammy sweating the morning after usually comes from your stress response being switched on. Low blood sugar, dehydration, nausea, and the nervous-system rebound after alcohol all release adrenaline, which causes sweating even when your skin feels cool. Eating something with carbohydrates, drinking fluids, and resting usually help. Cold sweats with chest pain, fainting, confusion, or repeated vomiting need urgent care.

**Can DHM help with night sweats after drinking?**

There is no good evidence that DHM prevents or treats night sweats. DHM has interesting animal research on how alcohol affects the brain's GABA system, which is involved in the rebound that can cause sweating, but human data are limited. It is not a fix for withdrawal sweats, and anyone sweating because they've stopped drinking heavily should see a doctor rather than rely on a supplement.
